lead: This unit explains the 8085 and 8086 microprocessors from the inside out: registers, flags, pins, machine cycles, bus modes, memory interfacing and string/control instructions. After it you can read an 8085 or 8086 block diagram, calculate a physical address, draw a basic timing diagram, decode a memory chip select and trace a REP MOVSB loop.
about: This unit moves from the 8085 to the 8086. Chapter 2.1 opens the 8085 block diagram, register set, flags and 40 pins. Chapter 2.2 turns register transfers into T-states and machine cycles with timing diagrams. Chapter 2.3 introduces the 8086 bus interface unit, execution unit, segment registers and signal groups. Chapter 2.4 shows how the same pins change role in minimum and maximum mode systems. Chapter 2.5 uses address decoding to place RAM and ROM chips in the memory map. Chapter 2.6 adds 8086 string and control transfer instructions for block moves and subroutine calls. The order builds from inside the CPU to the bus, then to memory and finally to programs that use the bus and stack.

chapters.idea: The 8085 is an 8-bit CPU whose registers, ALU, flags and control blocks communicate over one 8-bit internal bus.
chapters.depth: Cover the 8085 8-bit CPU: ALU, accumulator, temporary register, general registers B to L, PC and SP, instruction register/decoder, timing and control, interrupt control, serial I/O control, address buffer and address/data buffer. Give register widths: 8-bit general registers, 16-bit PC and SP, 8-bit flag register with S, Z, AC, P, CY. Draw and label the 40-pin DIP: address A15-A8, multiplexed AD7-AD0, ALE, RD, WR, IO/M, S0/S1, READY, HOLD/HLDA, RESET, CLK, interrupt pins, serial pins, power. Some syllabi call this 'functional building blocks of processor' or 'hardware architecture'. Keep interrupts at pin and block level.

figure.title: 8085 internal blocks
figure.aria: The 8085 internal blocks: instruction register feeds decoder, decoder feeds timing and control, registers feed ALU and data buffer, ALU sets the flag register, and timing control drives the address buffer.

chapters.example: The 8085 adds 9AH and 7CH. Give the accumulator content and the flag register bits S, Z, AC, P and CY.
chapters.trap: Forgetting that AC is the carry from bit 3 to bit 4, not the carry out of bit 7. Also 8085 parity is even parity: P = 1 only when the result has an even number of 1s.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: CPU, memory, buses and stored program concept.
chapters.leave: Memory interfacing to 2.5; full instruction set to Unit 3; full interrupt priority and vectoring to later study.

chapters.idea: Every 8085 instruction is a fixed sequence of T-states grouped into machine cycles, and the timing diagram shows what each bus line does in each T-state.
chapters.depth: Define T-state, machine cycle and instruction cycle. Show opcode fetch, memory read, memory write, I/O read and I/O write machine cycles for the 8085. Draw timing diagrams with CLK, A15-A8, AD7-AD0, ALE, RD, WR and IO/M. Count T-states for one-, two- and three-byte instructions. Some syllabi call these 'timing diagram' questions. Use MVI A, data as the two-machine-cycle case.

figure.title: MVI A, 32H: opcode fetch + memory read
figure.aria: Timing for MVI A, 32H: opcode fetch uses T1 to T4, memory read uses T5 to T7, ALE is high in T1 and T5, RD is low in T2 to T4 and T5 to T7, and AD7-AD0 carries address, opcode, address and data in turn.

chapters.example: The 8085 instruction MVI A, 32H is stored at address 2000H. Draw the opcode fetch and memory read machine cycles and count the total T-states.
chapters.trap: Mixing up ALE and RD timing: ALE is active in T1 of every machine cycle, while RD goes low only when data is read. Also MVI A, data is 2 bytes, so it needs 4 + 3 = 7 T-states, not 4.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1: 8085 registers, pins and control signals.
chapters.leave: Instruction encoding and addressing modes to Unit 3; 8086 bus timing to 2.4.

chapters.idea: The 8086 splits address generation from execution, so the bus interface unit fetches ahead while the execution unit works on earlier instructions.
chapters.depth: Cover 8086 architecture: Bus Interface Unit (BIU) with segment registers CS, DS, SS, ES, instruction pointer IP, address adder and 6-byte instruction queue; Execution Unit (EU) with general registers AX, BX, CX, DX, pointer/index registers SP, BP, SI, DI, ALU and flags. Explain 20-bit physical address = segment × 10H + offset. Describe signal groups: address/data, status, control, interrupt, DMA, clock and power. Some syllabi call this '8086 hardware architecture and signals'.

figure.title: 8086 BIU and EU
figure.aria: The 8086 bus interface unit holds segment registers, instruction pointer, address adder and instruction queue; the queue feeds the execution unit, which contains general registers and the ALU with flags.

chapters.example: The 8086 has CS = 1234H and IP = 0056H. Find the 20-bit physical address of the next instruction byte.
chapters.trap: Using decimal 10 instead of 10H in segment × 10H. Also CS pairs with IP for instruction fetch, while DS pairs with SI, DI or an offset for data.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: buses and registers; Chapter 2.1 for the 8-bit baseline.
chapters.leave: Pins and modes to 2.4; addressing modes to Unit 3; memory decoding to 2.5.

chapters.idea: The MN/MX pin decides whether the 8086 drives system control signals itself (minimum mode) or hands status to the 8288 bus controller (maximum mode).
chapters.depth: Explain the pins that change with MN/MX: in minimum mode the 8086 gives RD, WR, M/IO, DEN, DT/R, ALE, HOLD, HLDA; in maximum mode the 8086 gives status S2-S0 and control goes to the 8288 bus controller. Show minimum-mode system with 8284 clock, 8282 latches, 8286 transceivers and memory/I/O. Show maximum-mode system with 8288, latches and transceivers. Some syllabi call this 'min mode system configuration' and 'max mode system configuration'. Keep bus timing details to 2.2.

figure.title: 8086 minimum and maximum mode
figure.aria: The 8086 uses the 8284 clock, 8282 latches and 8286 transceivers in both modes; in maximum mode it sends status S2-S0 to the 8288 bus controller, which drives the control bus, while in minimum mode the 8086 drives control directly.

chapters.example: In a maximum-mode 8086 system the status lines are S2 S1 S0 = 101. Which 8288 output is active, and what bus operation does it perform?
chapters.trap: Learning pin names without the mode. ALE, DEN and DT/R are minimum-mode names; in maximum mode the same pins carry status S2-S0, and the 8288 produces the control signals.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.3: 8086 signals and BIU; Chapter 2.2 for bus timing.
chapters.leave: Detailed timing diagrams to 2.2; peripheral controllers 8255, 8259 and 8237 to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A memory chip is selected only when the high address lines match its base address, so a decoder turns address bits into chip-select signals.
chapters.depth: Cover memory map, chip select, address decoding with gates and the 74LS138 decoder, RAM and ROM interfacing, address range calculation and the number of address lines for a chip. Use 8085 and 8086 examples. Explain full decoding and partial decoding. Some syllabi call this '8085 architecture and memory interfacing (RAM & ROM)' or 'address decoding'.

figure.title: Address decoding for ROM and RAM
figure.aria: Address bus A15-A0 enters the 74LS138 decoder, whose outputs select the ROM at 0000H-07FFH and RAM at 2000H-27FFH; both chips connect to data bus D7-D0.

chapters.example: Interface a 2K x 8 EPROM and a 2K x 8 RAM to an 8085. The EPROM starts at 0000H and the RAM starts at 2000H. Give the address range of each chip and the number of address lines each chip needs.
chapters.trap: A 2K chip needs 11 address lines, because 2K = 2048 = 2^11. The range ends at start + 07FFH, not start + 0800H.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 2.1 and 2.2: address bus, control signals and machine cycles.
chapters.leave: I/O port interfacing and peripheral chips to Unit 5; 8051 memory to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: String instructions move or compare bytes through SI and DI with CX as counter, while control transfer instructions change IP or CS and IP.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Cover 8086 string instructions MOVS, CMPS, SCAS, LODS, STOS with REP prefixes and the direction flag DF. Cover control transfer: JMP, conditional jumps, CALL, RET, LOOP and INT. Show how CALL and RET use the stack to save IP and CS. Keep programs short: block copy and a delay loop. Some syllabi call this 'advanced instructions'.

figure.title: REP MOVSB loop
figure.aria: A REP MOVSB loop: if DF is 0, copy [SI] to AL and AL to [DI], increment SI and DI, decrement CX, and repeat until CX is 0; if DF is 1, decrement SI and DI instead.

chapters.example: A string of 5 bytes starts at DS:SI = 2000H:0100H. DI = 3000H, CX = 0005H, DF = 0. Give the physical addresses of the source and destination, and the values of SI, DI and CX after one MOVSB.
chapters.trap: With DF = 0, SI and DI increase; with DF = 1 they decrease. CX counts down after the move, so after one byte CX becomes 0004H, not 0005H.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3: addressing modes and stack; Chapter 2.3 for 8086 registers.
chapters.leave: Assembler syntax and full programming to Unit 3; 8051 serial interrupts to Unit 4.

links: 8085 register model leads to 8086 segment registers
read and write cycles set address and data timing
BIU and signals explain minimum and maximum mode pins
bus control signals drive memory chip selects
decoded memory holds string and stack data
machine cycle timing explains bus controller outputs
20-bit address generation sets the memory map
